items.title: Ignacio Berroa interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, October 22, 2021 [interview 2 of 2]
items.q: you have to check Max Roach, you should check Philly Joe Jones, you should check Art Blakey, those masters that came before us

ctx.x: sense of how it interacts. And I guess that must have paid dividends for you in that moment, because you were familiar not only with Dizzy but what his supporting sidemen were doing on those recordings.

Well that has paid big dividends in my career. Because I’m the type of drummer that always, I do a lot of listening. And I think that in my opinion, and from my experience, listening to music it is paramount. So you should listen to a lot of music, and when you listen to music, in my case I never concentrate on what the drummers were doing, I was — I listened to everything. And when I mean listened, listening, it’s not listening to an album just once. Because I have got students that I tell them you have to check…

I’m going to come back to that because it makes me think of the “Straight Ahead from Havana” that you sent. I wanted to ask, some bandleaders, I think most famously Count Basie, was known for not saying much to his musicians unless they really were behaving badly or playing badly. And I wonder if Dizzy spoke to you about what he wanted?
